hw3

  1. It is well-known that ridge regression tends to give similar coefficient values to correlated variables, whereas the lasso may give quite different coefficient values to correlated variables. We will now explore this property in a very simple setting. Suppose that n = 2, p = 2, x11 = x12, x21 = x22. Furthermore, suppose that y1 +y2 = 0 and x11 +x21 = 0 and x12 +x22 = 0, so that the estimate for the intercept in a least squares, ridge regression, or lasso model is zero: βˆ0 = 0.
  1. Write out the ridge regression optimization problem in this setting.
  2. Argue that in this setting, the ridge coefficient estimates satisfy βˆ1 = βˆ2.
  3. Write out the lasso optimization problem in this setting.
  4. Argue that in this setting, the lasso coefficients βˆ1 and βˆ2 are not unique—in other words, there are many possible solutions to the optimization problem in (c). Describe these solutions.
  1. In this exercise, we will generate simulated data, and will then use this data to perform best subset selection.
  1. Use the rnorm() function to generate a predictor X of length n = 100, as well as a noise vector ϵ of length n = 100.
X <- rnorm(100)
epsilon <- rnorm(100)
  1. Generate a response vector Y of length n = 100 according to the model Y = β0 + β1X + β2X2 + β3X3 + ϵ, where β0, β1, β2, and β3 are constants of your choice.
b_0 <- 5
b_1 <- 3
b_2 <- 6
b_3 <- 7
y <- b_0 + b_1*X + b_2*X^2 + b_3*X^3 + epsilon
  1. Use the regsubsets() function to perform best subset selection in order to choose the best model containing the predictors X, X2,…,X10. What is the best model obtained according to Cp, BIC, and adjusted R2? Show some plots to provide evidence for your answer, and report the coefficients of the best model obtained. Note you will need to use the data.frame() function to create a single data set containing both X and Y .
library(leaps)

set.seed(42)

df <- data.frame(y=y, x=X)
subset_fit <- regsubsets(y ~ I(X) + I(X^2)+ I(X^3) + I(X^4) + I(X^5) + I(X^6) + I(X^7) + I(X^8) + I(X^9) + I(X^10), data=df, nvmax=10)
reg_summary <- summary(subset_fit)

# Best model according to cp, bic, and adjr2
reg_cp <- which.min(reg_summary$cp)
reg_bic <- which.min(reg_summary$bic)
reg_adjr2 <- which.max(reg_summary$adjr2)

reg_cp
## [1] 3
reg_bic
## [1] 3
reg_adjr2
## [1] 3
# par(mfrow=c(2,2))

plot(subset_fit)

plot(reg_summary$adjr2 ,xlab="Number of Variables ", ylab="Adjusted RSq",type="l")
points(which.max(reg_summary$adjr2),reg_summary$adjr2[which.max(reg_summary$adjr2)], col="red",cex=2,pch=20)

plot(reg_summary$cp ,xlab="Number of Variables ",ylab="Cp", type='l')
points(which.min(reg_summary$cp),reg_summary$cp[which.min(reg_summary$cp)],col="red",cex=2,pch=20)

plot(reg_summary$bic ,xlab="Number of Variables ",ylab="BIC",type='l')
points(which.min(reg_summary$bic),reg_summary$bic[which.min(reg_summary$bic)],col="red",cex=2,pch=20)

# coefficients for best 3 variable model 
coef(subset_fit, 3)
## (Intercept)        I(X)      I(X^2)      I(X^3) 
##    5.112153    3.135779    5.964004    6.970476
  1. Repeat (c), using forward stepwise selection and also using backwards stepwise selection. How does your answer compare to the results in (c)?

Forward selection:

forward_fit <- regsubsets(y ~ I(X) + I(X^2)+ I(X^3) + I(X^4) + I(X^5) + I(X^6) + I(X^7) + I(X^8) + I(X^9) + I(X^10), data=df, nvmax=10, method="forward")
forward_summary <- summary(forward_fit)

# Best model according to cp, bic, and adjr2
which.min(forward_summary$cp)
## [1] 3
which.min(forward_summary$bic)
## [1] 3
which.max(forward_summary$adjr2)
## [1] 3
# coefficients for best 3 variable model 
coef(forward_fit, 3)
## (Intercept)        I(X)      I(X^2)      I(X^3) 
##    5.112153    3.135779    5.964004    6.970476

Backward selection:

backward_fit <- regsubsets(y ~ I(X) + I(X^2)+ I(X^3) + I(X^4) + I(X^5) + I(X^6) + I(X^7) + I(X^8) + I(X^9) + I(X^10), data=df, nvmax=10, method="backward")
backward_summary <- summary(backward_fit)

# Best model according to cp, bic, and adjr2
which.min(backward_summary$cp)
## [1] 3
which.min(backward_summary$bic)
## [1] 3
which.max(backward_summary$adjr2)
## [1] 3
# coefficients for best 3 variable model 
coef(backward_fit, 3)
## (Intercept)        I(X)      I(X^2)      I(X^3) 
##    5.112153    3.135779    5.964004    6.970476

The performance of each model tells us that a 3 variable model was the best model. The regular use of rsubsets() (neither forward nor backward stepwise) and the forward stepwise says that X, X^2, X^3, X^5, and X^10 were the best variables whereas the backwards stepwise says that X, X^2, X^3, X^5, and X^7 were the best variables.

  1. Now fit a lasso model to the simulated data, again using X, X2, …,X10 as predictors. Use cross-validation to select the optimal value of λ. Create plots of the cross-validation error as a function of λ. Report the resulting coefficient estimates, and discuss the results obtained.
library(glmnet)
## Loading required package: Matrix
## Loaded glmnet 4.1-10
X <- model.matrix(y ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3) + I(x^4) + I(x^5) + I(x^6) + I(x^7) + I(x^8) + I(x^9) + I(x^10), data=df)[, -1]
y <- df$y

set.seed(42)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X,y,alpha=1)
plot(cv_lasso, sign.lambda=1)

min.lambda <- cv_lasso$lambda.min
min.lambda
## [1] 0.3506202
prediction <- predict(cv_lasso, s = min.lambda, type = "coefficients")[1:11, ]
prediction
## (Intercept)           x      I(x^2)      I(x^3)      I(x^4)      I(x^5) 
##    5.626803    3.315387    5.487727    6.799078    0.000000    0.000000 
##      I(x^6)      I(x^7)      I(x^8)      I(x^9)     I(x^10) 
##    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000

The the model that uses lambda min only contains 5 out of the ten total predictors used: x, x^2, x^3, x^4, x^5. The Lasso method being used gives us information of what predictors are not useful by making them all 0.

  1. Now generate a response vector Y according to the model Y = β0 + β7X7 + ϵ, and perform best subset selection and the lasso. Discuss the results obtained.
set.seed(42)
X <- rnorm(100)
e <- rnorm(100)

b_0 <- 5
b_7 <- 3
y <- b_0 + b_7*X^7 + e

Best subset selection:

df <- data.frame(y=y, x=X)
diff_fit <- regsubsets(y ~ I(X) + I(X^2)+ I(X^3) + I(X^4) + I(X^5) + I(X^6) + I(X^7) + I(X^8) + I(X^9) + I(X^10), data=df, nvmax=10)
diff_summary <- summary(diff_fit)

# Best model according to cp, bic, and adjr2
which.min(diff_summary$cp)
## [1] 6
which.min(diff_summary$bic)
## [1] 4
which.max(diff_summary$adjr2)
## [1] 7
plot(diff_summary$adjr2 ,xlab="Number of Variables ", ylab="Adjusted RSq",type="l")
points(which.max(diff_summary$adjr2),diff_summary$adjr2[which.max(diff_summary$adjr2)], col="red",cex=2,pch=20)

plot(diff_summary$cp ,xlab="Number of Variables ",ylab="Cp", type='l')
points(which.min(diff_summary$cp),diff_summary$cp[which.min(diff_summary$cp)],col="red",cex=2,pch=20)

plot(diff_summary$bic ,xlab="Number of Variables ",ylab="BIC",type='l')
points(which.min(diff_summary$bic),diff_summary$bic[which.min(diff_summary$bic)],col="red",cex=2,pch=20)

# coefficients for best 4 variable model 
coef(diff_fit, 4)
##  (Intercept)       I(X^3)       I(X^5)       I(X^7)       I(X^9) 
##  4.879437515 -0.765855504  0.648983516  2.862371141  0.008358345

Lasso:

X <- model.matrix(y ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3) + I(x^4) + I(x^5) + I(x^6) + I(x^7) + I(x^8) + I(x^9) + I(x^10), data=df)[, -1]
y <- df$y

set.seed(42)
diff_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X,y,alpha=1)
plot(diff_lasso, sign.lambda=1)

min.lambda <- diff_lasso$lambda.min
min.lambda
## [1] 21.44145
prediction <- predict(diff_lasso, s = min.lambda, type = "coefficients")[1:11, ]
prediction
## (Intercept)           x      I(x^2)      I(x^3)      I(x^4)      I(x^5) 
##    1.773171    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000 
##      I(x^6)      I(x^7)      I(x^8)      I(x^9)     I(x^10) 
##    0.000000    2.912477    0.000000    0.000000    0.000000

In this instance, when the min lambda was used it only chose one predictor, x^7. This is because the response vector created in this problem contained x^7.

  1. In this exercise, we will predict the number of applications received using the other variables in the College data set.
  1. Split the data set into a training set and a test set.
require(ISLR)
## Loading required package: ISLR
data(College)
attach(College)

set.seed(42)

college_train = sample(1:nrow(College), nrow(College) * 0.7)
college_test = -college_train
y_test <- Apps[college_test]
  1. Fit a linear model using least squares on the training set, and report the test error obtained.
college_ols <- lm(Apps ~ ., data = College, subset = college_train)

summary(college_ols)

college_error
## [1] 1583501

The test MSE is 1583501

  1. Fit a ridge regression model on the training set, with λ chosen by cross-validation. Report the test error obtained.
matrix <- model.matrix(Apps~., data=College)[, -1]
matrix.train <- matrix[college_train,]
y <- College$Apps
y_train <- y[college_train]

ridge <- cv.glmnet(matrix.train, y_train, alpha=0)
plot(ridge, sign.lambda = 1)

ridge.lambda <- ridge$lambda.min

ridge_predict <- predict(ridge, s = ridge.lambda, newx = matrix[college_test, ])
ridge_error <- mean((ridge_predict - y_test)^2)
ridge_error
## [1] 2828195

The test error for ridge is 2828195.

  1. Fit a lasso model on the training set, with λ chosen by crossvalidation. Report the test error obtained, along with the number of non-zero coefficient estimates.
lasso <- cv.glmnet(matrix.train, y_train, alpha=1)
plot(lasso, sign.lambda=1)

lasso.lambda <- lasso$lambda.min
lasso.lambda
## [1] 12.77064

The min lambda for lasso is 9.660522

lasso_predict <- predict(lasso, s = lasso.lambda, newx = matrix[college_test, ])
lasso_error <- mean((lasso_predict - y_test)^2)
lasso_error
## [1] 1679044

The test MSE for lasso is 1675404

lasso.c <- predict(lasso,type="coefficients", s=lasso.lambda)[1:17,]
length(lasso.c[lasso.c != 0])
## [1] 15

Lasso produced 15 coefficient estimates that are not 0

  1. Comment on the results obtained. How accurately can we predict the number of college applications received? Is there much difference among the test errors resulting from these five approaches?
results <- c(college_error, ridge_error, lasso_error, pcr_error, pls_error)
names(results) <- c("lm", "ridge", "lasso", "pcr", "pls")
barplot(results)

print(sort(results))
##     pcr      lm     pls   lasso   ridge 
## 1583501 1583501 1594881 1679044 2828195

Ridge ended up performing the worst by having the highest error whereas the other four methods were within a small range of each other. PCR performed the best with having the lowest test error.
